common_name: Fairfax Wax Myrtle (Dense Upright Southern Bayberry Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fairfax is a dense, upright-growing wax myrtle selection well suited to hedging and screening in smaller garden spaces than the straight species.

directions: Fairfax is a selected, more compact and densely upright form of the Gulf Coast native southern wax myrtle, retaining the species' aromatic, glossy, blue-green foliage and tolerance of drought, salt spray, and poor sandy soils while staying tidier and better proportioned for hedges and mixed screens than seedling-grown plants. As with the species, it is a nitrogen-fixing, wildlife-friendly evergreen whose female plants produce waxy gray-blue berries valued by overwintering songbirds. Grow in full sun for the densest habit, though it also performs well with afternoon shade in hot climates; established plants need little supplemental water and respond well to light shearing to maintain a formal hedge line. Avoid heavy, poorly drained clay soils, which can shorten its lifespan compared with sandy or loamy sites.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Fairfax Gardening (Virginia Cooperative Extension Master Gardeners)

common_name: Aztec Fire Mexican Anise Tree (Dark Red-Flowered Illicium, J.C. Raulston Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist but well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Aztec Fire thrives with protection from harsh afternoon sun and benefits from a mulched root zone that stays evenly moist.

directions: Selected by plantsman J.C. Raulston, Aztec Fire is prized among Mexican anise tree forms for its unusually large, showy, dark burgundy-red flowers that appear intermittently from spring into fall, set against handsome, glossy dark-green, anise-scented foliage on a naturally pyramidal, evergreen shrub. It requires little pruning to maintain its neat form and makes an excellent specimen or woodland-edge planting where its striking flower color can be appreciated up close. Provide a sheltered site with consistently moist, well-drained, organically rich soil; while it tolerates full sun in cooler climates, it performs best with the light shade of high pine or hardwood canopy in the hotter Gulf South. Protect young plants from hard freezes until established, as this species is somewhat less cold-hardy than Illicium floridanum.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: White Florida Anise (Creamy White-Flowered Florida Anise Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; this white-flowered selection of Florida anise shares the species' preference for a shaded, evenly moist woodland site.

directions: 'Alba' is a creamy white-flowered form of the native Gulf Coast Florida anise, offering the same glossy, dark evergreen, anise-scented foliage and dense multi-stemmed habit as the maroon-flowered species but with pale, star-shaped blooms that show up more vividly against dark shade-garden foliage. It fills a valuable niche as one of the few flowering, shade-loving native evergreen shrubs, blooming in mid- to late spring while thriving in the same shaded, moist, acidic sites where the species is naturally found along Gulf Coast stream banks and ravines. Use it as a specimen, foundation planting, or informal hedge in dappled to deep shade, and keep the root zone consistently moist with organic mulch. As with the species, all plant parts are toxic if ingested.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown palms in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; give this form more room than typical dwarf palmetto since it slowly develops an above-ground trunk and a taller overall profile.

directions: This distinctive Louisiana and east Texas form of dwarf palmetto is found in a handful of swampy Gulf Coast populations and is set apart from typical Sabal minor by its bluish leaves and its slow but steady development of a true above-ground trunk, eventually taking on a form closer to a miniature cabbage palm than the usually stemless dwarf palmetto. It shares the species' exceptional cold hardiness, with reports of specimens surviving well below 0°F once established, making it a favorite among cold-hardy palm enthusiasts pushing a tropical look into the Upper South. Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and expect very slow growth, especially in the years before trunk formation begins; established plants tolerate periodic flooding and are extremely long-lived. Because trunk development takes many years, choose a permanent site and avoid transplanting large specimens.
